title: The Decision to Turn South
subtitle: A command decision before its military consequences
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: The German decision to redirect effort toward Ukraine, Guderian’s forces and the continuing Soviet defence of Kiev.
body:
On 21 August 1941, Hitler gave written priority to operations that would carry German forces away from an immediate assault on Moscow. The order placed the destruction of Soviet forces in Ukraine, the industrial resources of the Donets basin, the Crimea and the interruption of Caucasian oil supplies ahead of the capital. In the north, Leningrad and contact with Finland remained urgent objectives. This was a decision about how to use an army whose victories had enlarged its commitments faster than they had resolved them. The German leadership still expected a decisive outcome, but its senior commanders disagreed about which concentration of force could produce it. [1] The decision is best understood as a choice between operations whose feasibility depended on different assumptions about available strength and Soviet endurance. The southern case combined an exposed German flank with an opportunity to trap substantial armies. The Moscow proposal assumed that repairs, concentration and supporting flank operations could be completed in time for another decisive offensive. Soviet decisions also shaped the opportunity: German manoeuvre could produce an encirclement only if the opposing armies remained within reach of the routes it sought to sever. This chapter examines those interacting judgements, separating the written decision from its execution and from the later outcomes through which it has often been interpreted.

The Moscow proposal and its conditions

The immediate alternative to Hitler’s decision was developed in the German Army High Command’s memorandum of 18 August. It argued that the main surviving Soviet strength stood before Moscow and that a concentrated offensive there offered the best chance of decisive destruction. The capital’s importance as a political centre and communications hub reinforced this operational argument. Nevertheless, the memorandum was a plan for an offensive after preparation, rather than evidence that a fully supplied army could simply resume the advance that afternoon. Its timetable and force allocations reveal how much remained to be accomplished. [1] The proposed southern assault group was particularly substantial: twelve infantry divisions and six armoured or motorised divisions would attack on an approximately eighty-mile front between the Bryansk and Roslavl areas toward Kaluga. Farther north, separate groupings would move through the approaches to Bely and Rzhev. Ten infantry divisions would hold the broad intervening sector east of Smolensk. This was an attempt to turn a geographically dispersed army group into converging assault forces. It required assembly, coordination and the protection of the intervening front, not merely the selection of a direction on a map. [1] The timetable also depended on battles outside the proposed main axis. The fighting around Gomel was supposed to be successfully concluded by 23 August. An operation around Velikiye Luki was to begin on the twenty-first. Repairs were expected to make the mobile formations available toward the end of the month, with the main offensive possible early in September. Each condition could affect the others. A division held near Gomel could not simultaneously assemble for an attack toward Kaluga; a vehicle waiting for an engine could not transport ammunition simply because its formation had been assigned a new objective. [1] The memorandum’s preference for concentration acknowledged the limited movement that emergency rehabilitation would restore. Its answer was to use the remaining mobile strength in a decisive central operation before the campaigning season narrowed further. That argument depended partly on Army Groups North and South completing their tasks without substantial additional assistance. The counterattacks discussed in The War Widens had already tested that premise by drawing resources into the northern sector. Concentration on Moscow was therefore a proposal to accept and manage risks elsewhere, with consequences that must be evaluated alongside the prospective gain on the main axis. [1]

The southern flank as an operational problem

The southern alternative grew from the relationship between Army Groups Centre and South. As Centre advanced eastward through Belarus, its right flank extended beyond the forces operating in Ukraine. Soviet formations around Gomel and farther south could threaten the communications behind the advancing German armies. Their continued presence also obstructed a direct connection between the two army groups. The issue was therefore both defensive and offensive: securing German communications might create the opportunity to strike behind the Soviet armies defending the Dnieper and Kiev. [2] The Soviet 5th Army was central to this calculation. Operating north and northwest of Kiev, it had complicated Army Group South’s progress while remaining vulnerable to a movement descending from the north. Hitler’s instructions sought a concentric operation by the adjoining wings of the two army groups to prevent Soviet forces escaping eastward. Army Group Centre was to provide the forces necessary for that task even if doing so delayed a subsequent operation elsewhere. This requirement changed the scale of the commitment: the southward movement became an operational priority in its own right. [1] Gomel’s fall did not eliminate the work between decision and execution. As the preceding study showed, Soviet troops were still fighting east of the city and around the Sozh and Iput crossings after German forces entered it. For Weichs’s 2nd Army and Guderian’s 2nd Panzer Group, moving farther south meant crossing additional rivers, controlling junctions and securing the routes behind the leading formations. The infantry army’s position and the panzer group’s movements had to be related to each other, even though their speeds and supply requirements differed. [3] The Moscow plan itself provided for a substantial covering force east of Gomel and troops in the Pripyat region. Both proposals therefore addressed the southern flank, but assigned different scales and purposes to the response. A limited securing operation aimed to protect the central offensive while preserving its main concentration. A deeper movement towards the rear of Kiev sought a major result in the south and accepted delay elsewhere. The disagreement concerned the force required, the risk that could be tolerated and the value of the expected outcome. Those distinctions make the alternatives more precise than a choice between recognising and ignoring the flank. [1]

Time in the strategic calculation

A staff officer’s calendar

Blau’s reconstruction records Warlimont’s 18 August estimate that roughly eight weeks remained for northern operations and thirteen for those in the south before winter. The figures supported his recommendation to concentrate on Moscow, even if some flank and rear dangers had to be accepted. They were planning judgements about a shrinking interval, rather than forecasts of conditions on every road. The estimate reveals how advocates of the central offensive framed the opportunity cost of diversion: time spent elsewhere could consume the period in which their preferred operation remained practicable. It does not establish that the risks they proposed accepting would have remained manageable.

[1]

Resources, objectives and the enemy still in the field

Hitler’s reply incorporated a different conception of how the Soviet Union could be defeated. The Donets basin offered an industrial target, the Crimea threatened the security of the Romanian oil region through Soviet air operations, and a further movement toward the Caucasus promised pressure on Soviet oil supplies. These objectives joined military geography to the economic foundations of the war. They also extended the scale of the undertaking. Destroying an army west of the Dnieper, occupying an industrial region and cutting a distant petroleum supply were connected ambitions, but success in one did not automatically accomplish the others. [1] Hitler’s concern for the Crimea connected the southern operation to Romania’s importance as a source of petroleum. Soviet aircraft operating from the peninsula presented a threat to those oilfields in his assessment, giving its capture a place within Germany’s wider war economy. Translating that priority into conquest would require a distinct commitment of troops, engineering and supply. The strategic problem was consequently one of sequence as well as purpose: protecting a valuable resource could draw forces into an operation whose demands competed with those of destroying Soviet armies elsewhere. The economic argument identified a reason to act without resolving the means or timing. [1] The northern priority imposed another competing demand. Leningrad was to be isolated and contact established with Finnish forces. German plans also linked the eventual Moscow offensive to the release of formations and air support from the northern operation. This interdependence made the apparent sequence fragile. If the north required longer than expected, forces promised for the centre would remain unavailable; if Soviet counterattacks forced additional German reinforcement, the sequence could become a further redistribution. The directive of 21 August expressed a hierarchy of objectives, but it could not guarantee that the enemy would permit them to be completed in that order. [1] The rival proposals also defined the mechanism of decision differently. Army leaders placed greater emphasis on destroying the forces believed to be concentrated before Moscow. Hitler joined destruction in Ukraine to the seizure or denial of resources supporting Soviet resistance. Both required assumptions about how military loss would affect the state’s ability to continue. Earlier encirclements had not prevented new armies from appearing, and occupation of industrial territory could yield less usable production if machinery had been removed or destroyed. The planners therefore had to connect the immediate operation to a wider process of collapse whose conditions their victories had yet to establish. [1]

Guderian and the movement that followed

The competing plans also expose the importance of engineering and transport without requiring a single misleading estimate for the whole front. The Moscow proposal envisaged several assault groupings operating on separate axes, a broad holding sector and a distinct flank-covering army. Each grouping required its own ammunition delivery, fuel distribution and maintenance arrangements, while the supporting railway system had to feed the combined effort. Concentrating combat power did not mean that every supporting activity could be concentrated at one place. The plan’s readiness date represented an attempt to bring these different requirements into alignment. [1] The southern operation substituted a different set of demands. Connections between Centre and South had to be established across the operational space still occupied by Soviet troops. Bridges and roads had to remain usable after the assault formations passed, and forces guarding them needed supplies as well. The likely gain was a more secure junction between army groups and the destruction of an enemy concentration. The immediate price was additional movement and another period in which workshops and transport columns had to support formations operating farther from their previous assembly areas. This was a resource allocation decision within an already active campaign. [1] Guderian’s role needs to be placed within this sequence rather than made its sole explanation. His 2nd Panzer Group supplied the principal mobile instrument for the southward operation. On 23 August, after the written decision had been issued, he met Hitler in an attempt to reopen the argument. Halder and Bock hoped that the commander’s direct account of his troops and their prospects might support a renewed concentration toward Moscow. The attempt failed to reverse the decision. The date matters: the meeting was a subsequent effort to alter an established priority, not the occasion on which the original written order was issued. [2] The resulting movement did not carry every formation associated with Guderian in a single intact block. The operational account records that much of his infantry and a panzer corps remained to protect the flank under Kluge’s 4th Army while the striking force moved south. Such allocations expose the cost of changing direction. A headquarters could receive a large objective while its immediately available force was reduced by the obligation to cover the space it had already crossed. Mobile warfare produced vulnerable communications as well as opportunities for further penetration. [2] By 25 August, the German 2nd Army and 2nd Panzer Group were beginning the larger southward operation. Their movement would develop toward the routes behind the Soviet Southwestern Front, with the panzer group eventually driving toward Romny. That destination describes the developing operation; it should not be placed under German control on 21 August. Nor should the later junction with forces advancing north from Army Group South be treated as an accomplished fact at the moment of decision. The September encirclement required additional advances, crossings and Soviet decisions that still lay ahead. [2] Changing the direction of advance also changed the relationship between leading formations and their support. Infantry protecting an earlier flank, workshops repairing vehicles and transport columns supplying a new axis could occupy widely separated positions. Further penetration increased the work needed to keep those elements connected. The German documents’ repeated concern with repair and flank protection shows that commanders understood this constraint even while disagreeing about the next objective. Their usable force was determined by the tasks and condition of its parts. The reach of a leading armoured detachment consequently cannot represent the readiness of the whole grouping for another operation. [1]

What Moscow understood, and what Kiev was ordered to hold

Soviet command was not wholly unaware of the southern danger. On 19 August, Shaposhnikov informed Zhukov that he and Stalin accepted the likelihood of a German movement southward. The Southwestern Direction and the fronts concerned were warned, while instructions continued to insist on holding Kiev and the Dnieper line. This combination is more revealing than a simple claim that Stalin either knew nothing or knew everything. The warning identified a possible enemy intention; it did not settle how much ground should be abandoned, how quickly an army could withdraw or which danger deserved immediate priority. [2] The Soviet command also took measures to protect the threatened junction. The Bryansk Front had been established under Andrei Eremenko during the middle of August, initially with the danger to the Moscow direction prominent in its responsibilities. As German forces turned south, the relationship between that front and the neighbouring armies became increasingly important. A new front headquarters could concentrate responsibility and coordinate reserves, but its existence did not itself provide the trained troops, communications or freedom of movement required to stop a panzer group. Organisational adaptation and operational capability developed on different schedules. [2] There were also authorised withdrawals. The Southwestern Direction’s order of 19 August instructed the 5th Army to begin moving behind the Dnieper during the night of 19–20 August and provided for a northern defensive flank toward the Chernigov area. It specified the use of divisions for that protection and referred to the 293rd Rifle Division arriving by rail near Sumy. These were concrete attempts to reposition forces while preserving the larger defence. Their limitations became apparent when the enemy threatened routes farther east than the line the army had been ordered to occupy. [4] Retaining Kiev preserved a defended crossing region within the Dnieper position, but its value depended on the communications of the armies around it remaining usable. A penetration descending farther east could change that calculation before troops defending the city experienced an immediate tactical defeat. The Soviet command’s problem therefore lay in converting recognition of a possible threat into timely authority for an adequate response. Warnings and local withdrawals demonstrate awareness, while continued instructions to hold show the limits imposed on action. Their interaction explains the developing danger more accurately than a claim that knowledge alone would have prevented it. [2] Contemporary warnings and orders provide a firmer basis for examining this process than a single retrospective conversation presented as decisive. They establish that the southern danger was discussed before 21 August and that the defence of Kiev and the Dnieper remained an obligation. They leave differences in information, assessment and practical freedom between commands to be reconstructed. Withdrawal itself would have required routes, transport and protection under enemy pressure. The failure was therefore a failure to produce an adequate operational response through the available command system, with its timing and restrictions considered, rather than simply a failure to utter a warning.

The command climate and the people beneath it

Order No. 270, issued on 16 August, formed part of the coercive setting in which Soviet commanders and soldiers faced these decisions. It instructed encircled formations to continue fighting and break through to their own troops. At the same time, it treated surrender and desertion through sweeping accusations against named officers and threatened severe punishment. Commanders and political officers classed as malicious deserters were to be shot, and their families arrested. Families of ordinary soldiers who surrendered were to lose state assistance. These were explicit measures of collective punishment, not simply appeals for military determination. [5] Order No. 270 used named officers to make an exemplary disciplinary argument. Its accusations should be treated as assertions within that purpose, rather than findings established by an independent investigation. The order narrowed the distinction between military defeat and personal culpability, threatening punishment for conduct that superiors might interpret as abandonment or betrayal. For officers in a deteriorating situation, this added political consequences to decisions about withdrawal, separation and surrender. The document cannot explain every individual’s choice, but it establishes a coercive framework that must be considered alongside the operational demands imposed by the enemy. [5] For civilian households, the same policy extended military events into the conditions of survival at home. A soldier’s capture could threaten a family’s material support; an officer’s classification could expose relatives to arrest. The threatened penalties were especially consequential in a war already disrupting wages, housing and access to food. The state demanded continued resistance while making families answerable for actions they could neither observe nor control. This aspect of Soviet policy belongs in the history of the battlefield because it shaped the consequences of defeat beyond the men physically present in an encirclement. [5] German plans exposed civilians to a different, separately documented threat. The supplement to Directive No. 34, issued on 12 August, had halted a direct assault on Kiev while envisaging the city’s destruction by incendiary bombing and artillery when the necessary means became available. This was an intention in an operational directive, not evidence that the contemplated destruction had already occurred. Nevertheless, it shows how the civilian city entered German planning as a target to be devastated rather than merely a position to be bypassed. The distinction between military manoeuvre and violence against urban life was already breaking down within the instructions themselves. [1]

Schoolbooks on an evacuation train

Agnessa Margolina recalled leaving Kiev with relatives in August 1941. In her 2003 interview for Centropa, she described carrying her four-year-old cousin Boris while her stepmother carried a suitcase. Her brothers brought textbooks for the next school year. The family travelled independently of a workplace evacuation, boarding a crowded freight train fitted with plank sleeping platforms. Her account remembers bombing, interruptions and uncertainty about the destination.

The interview does not establish an exact departure day, and some of its later dates and geographical details are inconsistent. Its account of the family’s luggage should therefore remain an attributed recollection. The schoolbooks nevertheless illuminate a recognisably different scale of planning from that of the headquarters: children preparing to continue an interrupted education while adults tried to move a multigenerational household beyond the fighting. Their escape depended on the same railway capacity that the armies and evacuated factories also required. [6]

An expanding war economy

The strategic argument in Germany coincided with a different discussion about resources among the Soviet Union, Britain and the United States. On 18 August, the State Department transmitted the signed Roosevelt–Churchill message proposing a conference in Moscow to consider future assistance. The message explicitly described a long struggle and acknowledged that even substantial British and American resources were limited. Allocation required decisions about competing fronts, manufactured equipment and raw materials. Its significance lay in the attempt to organise sustained cooperation, rather than in any immediate transformation of Soviet combat strength. [7] The United States was still outside the war as a belligerent. Its participation in this planning nevertheless widened the economic horizon against which Germany’s calculations had to be judged. Hitler sought to deprive the Soviet Union of resources and secure Germany’s position; Roosevelt and Churchill proposed coordinating resources to sustain Soviet resistance. These processes operated at different speeds. A shipment promised, loaded or at sea could not substitute for ammunition at an army’s gun positions. The joint message itself distinguished immediate shipments from the longer programme to be negotiated, a distinction essential to understanding what diplomacy could and could not accomplish in August. [7] The relationship between these economic strategies makes the Moscow counterfactual difficult to resolve with confidence. David Stahel argues that German losses, overextension and Soviet endurance had already undermined the campaign’s original assumptions, and he challenges a narrative in which an otherwise attainable victory was lost through one diversion. His introduction to Kiev 1941 also emphasises the influence of German postwar memoirs on that interpretation. This does not make every alternative equally plausible or remove the costs of the southward operation. It does require the historian to examine what the army could sustain, what the enemy could still do and how much a captured objective would actually change. [8] The Moscow alternative remains historically significant because it reveals what senior commanders believed could still be achieved. Assessing it requires specifying the formations, repairs, supply arrangements and flank protection on which the proposal depended, and the Soviet forces likely to oppose it. It also requires defining the proposed result: occupying the capital, destroying its defending armies and ending the Soviet capacity to fight were distinct achievements. The 18 August memorandum supplies evidence for intentions and assumptions, not proof that all the conditions would have been fulfilled. The cost of the southern decision can consequently be examined without treating the unexecuted operation as a secured victory. [1]

A decision whose outcome remained open

On 21 August, the German leadership had selected a priority; it had not yet secured the result. The southward operation promised to join the advances of two army groups against Soviet forces whose northern flank was increasingly exposed. It also committed mobile formations to another substantial movement while repairs, replacements and communications remained under strain. Guderian’s unsuccessful intervention on the twenty-third and the opening of the larger advance on the twenty-fifth belong to the execution of that choice. The eventual September encirclement belongs to a further stage of the campaign. [2] The Soviet position was equally unresolved. Warnings existed, limited withdrawals had been ordered, and a new front headquarters was attempting to organise the threatened sector. Yet Kiev and the Dnieper remained positions to be held, while punitive orders made the consequences of failure reach into soldiers’ families. Beyond both command systems were people trying to keep factories operating, find transport, preserve households and escape the advance. The next study closes this phase by examining the front on 25 August: an army turning south, other battles continuing elsewhere, and a war whose demands were expanding faster than either side could bring them under control.

sourceMethod: Unpublished review draft. Numbered references link to the bibliography and return to their first use. Specific document, paragraph and page locators accompany the references. Soviet military records were read in Russian transcription from the published General Staff collections; English descriptions are paraphrases by the atlas, and archival identifiers are those printed in the collections, not claims of direct archival inspection. Orders establish intentions; situation reports contain contemporary information, estimates and gaps. U.S. Army retrospective studies are read critically alongside Soviet records and other scholarship. Publisher excerpts are cited only for inspected passages. Testimony is distinguished from contemporary reporting. Dates in titles anchor the chronology; subsequent developments are dated explicitly. The atlas layers are qualified regional interpretations; their boundaries and arrows are not independent evidence of exact control or unit positions.
